title: Retinocortical in-sensor neuromorphic vision platform for NIR-augmented artificial vision

paper_content.abstract: In-sensor neuromorphic vision platforms with near-infrared (NIR) sensitivity are essential for intelligent imaging in low-light and multispectral environments. Here, a retinocortical dual-mode platform based on evolved-synaptic transistor (Evo-SynT) devices using upconversion nanoparticles (UCNP) and their integration into evolved-retina optical synapse (EROS) arrays is introduced. Evo-SynT devices exhibit key synaptic features, including paired-pulse facilitation indices exceeding 183.93% and 136.36% at a 0.5 s interval under 808 nm and 940 nm illumination, respectively, and analog weight modulation across 512 conductance states. A 12×12 EROS array enables dual-mode operation: retinal-like in-sensor preprocessing and cortical-like in-memory classification. The EROS array improves pedestrian detection accuracy under low-light conditions from 0.7806 to 0.8481 (808 nm) and 0.9071 (940 nm), and achieves classification accuracies of 77.19% and 79.40%, respectively. These results highlight the EROS platform as a scalable solution for integrated NIR-sensitive neuromorphic vision systems.
paper_content.introduction:
The human visual system processes optical information through a hierarchical retinocortical pathway, where photoreceptors in the retina perform early-stage analog signal preprocessing, and the visual cortex conducts higher-order feature extraction and cognitive interpretation, as shown in Fig. 1a. Inspired by this biological model, artificial vision systems are increasingly adopting architectures that emulate both retinal and cortical functions in hardware, bridging early signal acquisition with downstream intelligence.1-4 Such bioinspired retinocortical frameworks offer a promising foundation for developing next-generation vision computing platforms that operate beyond the visible spectrum. Indeed, while biological vision remains fundamentally constrained to visible wavelengths, artificial vision systems can exploit spectral regions such as near-infrared (NIR), which hold significant untapped potential for advanced perception.5-7

Extending artificial vision capabilities into the NIR range (~700-1000 nm) enables access to rich visual information beyond human perception. NIR light penetrates materials opaque to visible wavelengths, allowing imaging in low-light, dark, or visually obstructed conditions. This spectral advantage has driven the deployment of NIR-sensitive systems in fields such as autonomous driving, biomedical imaging, remote sensing, and security surveillance.8-11 However, while sensing in this regime is well established, the challenge lies in processing large volumes of data in real time. Conventional architectures, which separate sensing and computation, often suffer from latency and bandwidth limitations. In response, in-sensor vision computing platforms are emerging as an effective solution, co-locating sensing and processing to enable immediate, energy-efficient interpretation of NIR visual data.12-16

Realizing such integrated NIR sensing and processing platforms at the device level critically depends on the intrinsic capabilities of the underlying semiconductor materials. Various emerging semiconductor candidates for NIR in-sensor vision computing, such as two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors and organic compounds, offer appealing advantages including strong light–matter interactions, mechanical flexibility, and tunable spectral responses.17-20 However, despite these promising attributes, both 2D and organic semiconductors face critical drawbacks in achieving large-area integration, as well as stable and uniform operation—essential requirements for practical vision applications.21-23 As a result, meeting the practical requirements of NIR in-sensor vision systems has remained a significant challenge.

In light of these limitations, metal-oxide semiconductors have drawn renewed interest as an alternative material platform for in-sensor vision computing devices. Metal-oxide semiconductors offer high electronic performance, excellent uniformity over large-area substrates, and good environmental stability, directly addressing the scalability and stability challenges of 2D and organic semiconductors.24-30,48,49 However, most metal-oxide semiconductors possess wide bandgaps. For instance, indium gallium zinc oxide (IGZO) exhibits a band gap of approximately 3.3 eV, which makes it effectively unresponsive to NIR light. This inherent limitation means that metal-oxide-based sensors cannot directly detect NIR signals, representing a critical drawback for NIR in-sensor vision computing applications.

In this research, we demonstrate a metal-oxide-based in-sensor vision computing platform, termed the evolved-retina optical synapse (EROS) array, which enables direct NIR signal detection and subsequent image processing within the array. The EROS array consists of a 12×12 pixel matrix, with each pixel comprising an IGZO-based evolved-synaptic transistor (Evo-SynT)—in which upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) convert incident NIR photons into ultraviolet (UV) or visible wavelengths detectable by the metal- oxide semiconductor, as shown in Fig. 1b. This design endows each pixel with direct NIR sensitivity at 808 nm and 940 nm, enabling reliable image acquisition under low-light conditions beyond the visible spectrum. Furthermore, by leveraging the uniform, large-area deposition of metal-oxide-based electronics, the EROS array achieves consistent performance across all pixels, overcoming the scalability and uniformity limitations of prior 2D- or organic-based devices. As shown in Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 1, this platform operates in dual modes—retina-like preprocessing for enhancing NIR imagery in low-visibility conditions, and cortex-like neuromorphic postprocessing for generating analog synaptic outputs suitable for subsequent neural network-based classification. These findings demonstrate a near-infrared sensitive in-sensor vision computing platform that integrates early-stage signal acquisition with downstream information processing, offering a viable route toward machine vision systems that operate beyond the spectral range of human perception.
paper_content.results:
Upconversion enabled near infrared synaptic behavior
To enable NIR photoresponsivity in the Evo-SynT, UCNPs were employed as internal spectral converters. UCNPs are luminescent nanomaterials that convert NIR light into higher-energy UV or visible emissions through a multiphoton process known as photon upconversion.31 Typically built from a NaYF4 host lattice doped with Yb3+ sensitizers and activator ions such as Tm3+ or Er3+, UCNPs exhibit sharp emission peaks, long lifetimes, and high photostability.32,33 Among various UCNP candidates, NaYF4 co-doped with Yb and Tm (NaYF4:Yb/Tm) nanoparticles were introduced due to their ability to emit UV and blue photons, which spectrally overlap with the optical absorption range of IGZO, enabling efficient photocarrier generation under upconverted illumination.34 NaYF4:Yb/Tm nanoparticles were synthesized via thermal decomposition in oleic acid and 1-octadecene, a well-established route for producing monodisperse nanocrystals with high upconversion efficiency. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and dynamic light scattering (DLS) confirmed a uniform spherical morphology with an average diameter of 34 ± 1.3 nm (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2 ). Elemental mapping using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) revealed homogeneous spatial distribution of Y, F, Yb, and Tm ions across the surface (Fig. 2d), with quantitative analysis indicating doping levels of 6.21% Yb and 0.99% Tm consistent with commonly used doping levels for efficient upconversion and minimal concentration quenching.35

To evaluate the upconversion property of UCNPs, photoluminescence (PL) spectrum of the synthesized NaYF4:Yb/Tm nanoparticles were measured under 980 nm NIR laser excitation at a power intensity of 500 mW cm-2, as shown in Fig. 2b. Under 980 nm excitation, the UCNPs exhibited sharp photoluminescence peaks at 344 nm (1I6 → 3F4), 360 nm (1D2 → 3H6), 450 nm (1D2 → 3F4), and 473 nm (1G4 → 3H6), which are characteristic of Tm3+ transitions.34 These emissions result from sequential energy transfer between Yb3+ sensitizers and Tm3+ activators. In this system, Yb3+ acts as a sensitizer: upon absorbing 980 nm photons, Yb3+ ions are excited from the 2F7/2 to the 2F5/2 level and subsequently transfer their energy to neighboring Tm3+ ions (Fig. 2c).36 These results confirm the upconversion functionality of the NaYF4:Yb/Tm nanoparticles, whereby absorbed NIR photons are converted into higher-energy emissions through multiphoton excitation processes.

Based on the verified optical functionality and structural uniformity of the NaYF4:Yb/Tm nanoparticles, the Evo-SynT device was fabricated by embedding the UCNPs between two IGZO active layers, as shown in Fig. 2e. The detailed fabrication process is described in Supplementary Fig. 3 and the methods section. This embedded structure maximizes photonic interaction within the active region while minimizing interfacial degradation, enhances photon-to-carrier conversion efficiency, and ensures long-term stability under optical stimulation by confining the upconverted emissions near the IGZO interface. UV–Vis–NIR absorption measurements further confirmed this optical enhancement, with the IGZO/UCNP/IGZO sandwich structure exhibiting substantially higher absorbance in the 808 and 940 nm regions compared to pristine IGZO film or IGZO/UCNP bilayers (Supplementary Fig. 4), validating the effectiveness of the vertical stacking strategy for NIR light harvesting.

To evaluate the device-level photoresponse of the upconversion-assisted Evo-SynT, transfer characteristics were measured under NIR irradiation at 808 nm and 940 nm with VDS of 10.1 V. As shown in Fig. 2f and 2g, the device exhibited increasing drain current and negative shift with rising optical power at both wavelengths, confirming NIR responsiveness. These observations verify that the integrated UCNPs play a central role in enabling deep NIR sensitivity in the Evo-SynT. To confirm that the upconverted light emitted by the UCNPs can be effectively absorbed by the IGZO channel, the optical absorption characteristics of IGZO were analyzed. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, the Tauc plot extracted from ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) spectroscopy reveals an optical bandgap of approximately 3.21 eV, which corresponds to the absorption of photons in the ultraviolet and blue spectral regions. This result confirms that the upconverted emissions from the UCNPs fall within the absorbable energy range of the IGZO channel.

To quantify this energy transfer efficiency, we performed a spectral overlap–based analysis. We defined the optical coupling efficiency (ηcoupling) as the ratio of the absorbed photon flux to the total emitted flux, calculated by integrating the overlap between the UCNP emission spectrum and the IGZO spectral absorptance:
𝜂coupling = (∫ΦUCNP(𝜆) 𝐴IGZO(𝜆) 𝑑𝜆 / ∫ΦUCNP(𝜆) 𝑑𝜆) ×100 (%)

where ΦUCNP(𝜆) represents the UCNP photon flux spectrum and 𝐴IGZO(𝜆) is the wavelength dependent absorption probability of the IGZO channel.

This calculation yields an estimated ηcoupling of approximately 21.6%, confirming that the dominant NaYF4:Yb/Tm emission peaks (e.g., 290 nm, 345 nm, 360 nm) are effectively harvested by the active layer. Crucially, while typical NaYF4:Yb/Tm systems exhibit a modest internal upconversion quantum yield (UCQY) of 0.5–4%, the high optical coupling combined with the intrinsic photoconductive gain of the transistor compensates for the limited photon flux.32,33,52,53 The UV and blue photons generated by UCNPs possess sufficient energy to excite trap states associated with deep-level neutral oxygen vacancies (VO) within the IGZO channel. Upon photoexcitation, deep-level neutral VO centers are ionized into donor-like states such as VO+ and VO2+ near the conduction band, releasing electrons into the channel (e.g., VO0 → VO+ + e- or VO0 → VO2+ + 2e-), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 6. This process significantly increases channel conductivity under illumination. Furthermore, the ionized VO states are metastable, and their recombination is kinetically hindered, leading to a prolonged photocurrent decay even after the removal of light.37,38,50 This persistent photoconductance (PPC) behavior enables the device to retain optical memory, supporting its operation as a photo-synaptic element in neuromorphic vision systems. This PPC mechanism, involving VO ionization and slow recombination kinetics, is consistent with prior observations in IGZO, further validating the oxygen vacancy origin of PPC in Evo-SynT.51

To confirm that the NIR photoresponse originates specifically from the UCNP-mediated upconversion process, control devices without UCNPs or with only the dispersing solvent were tested, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 7. Both configurations showed negligible response under 808 nm and 940 nm illumination, validating that the observed photocurrent in Evo-SynT is exclusively attributed to the upconverted emissions from NaYF4:Yb/Tm nanoparticles. To further ensure that the observed photocurrent does not originate from thermal effects but exclusively from the upconversion process, we additionally conducted in-situ temperature measurements under prolonged 808 nm illumination at a power density of 1 W/mm2 for 10,000 s. The p+-Si/SiO2/IGZO was tested. The sample exhibited a temperature increase from 24.35 oC to 47.77 oC, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 8. Considering that typical measurement durations are on the order of 10 s, during which the temperature remained close to room temperature, these results confirm that the photoresponse is not thermally driven but is a direct consequence of UCNP-mediated upconversion.

To investigate the synaptic behavior of the upconversion-assisted Evo-SynT, its ability to retain photocurrent after pulsed optical stimulation was first examined. Postsynaptic current (PSC) measurements were performed under pulsed NIR illumination at 808 nm and 940 nm with VDS = 0.5 V. As shown in Fig. 2h and 2j, 808 nm and 940 nm light pulses were applied for 5 s, under varying power densities, and the drain current was monitored for 60 s following light-off. In both wavelength regimes, the device exhibited a power-dependent increase in peak PSC followed by a gradual decay, indicative of synaptic relaxation behavior. The inset graph in Fig. 2h and 2j shows the extracted PSC values measured 60 s after light-off for each power condition. To more clearly visualize the retention behavior, the PSC values at 70 s were plotted as a function of optical intensity in Fig. 2i and 2k. Starting from an initial dark current of approximately 0.05 nA, the PSC increased from 0.21 nA to 2.15 nA under 808 nm, and from 0.18 nA to 0.71 nA under 940 nm, as the power intensity increased from 13 mW mm-2 to 1325 mW mm-2. These results demonstrate that the Evo-SynT can function as a photo-synaptic element capable of encoding input strength into persistent electrical states, validating its potential for vision-inspired neuromorphic computing.

Demonstration of upconversion enabled synaptic functionality
To comprehensively evaluate the synaptic functionality of the upconversion-assisted Evo-SynT, a series of electrical measurements were performed under NIR optical stimulation. These include paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) to probe short-term plasticity (STP), transition from STP to long-term potentiation (LTP) under repeated stimuli, as well as reversible potentiation/depression cycles and conductance linearity—collectively demonstrating the device’s capacity to emulate essential forms of learning and memory at the hardware level.39,40

As an initial indicator of STP, PPF measurements were conducted under pulsed NIR illumination at 808 nm and 940 nm, as shown in Fig. 3a. PPF, a characteristic STP response, reflects enhanced PSC upon a second stimulus due to residual carrier effects. The PPF index is quantitatively defined as:
PPF index (%) = (A2/A1)×100

where A1 and A2 represent the amplitudes of the first and second postsynaptic current peaks, respectively. The device exhibited a maximum PPF index of 183.93% at 0.5 s under 808 nm, and 136.36% at the same interval under 940 nm. In both cases, the PPF index decayed exponentially with increasing inter-pulse interval (ΔT), consistent with biologically inspired facilitation dynamics. These findings confirm that the Evo-SynT reliably reproduces STP behavior under optical stimulation.

To explore the transition from STP to LTP, a fundamental mechanism underlying learning and memory, key stimulation parameters were systematically modulated under 808 nm and 940 nm excitation. First, the PSC was measured at increasing pulse frequencies while maintaining a constant light power density of 13 mW mm-2, revealing frequency dependent synaptic potentiation as shown in Fig. 3b and 3c. Under 808 nm, the PSC increased from 0.19 nA at 0.2 Hz to 0.61 nA at 1 Hz, while 940 nm excitation resulted in a rise from 0.06 nA to 0.23 nA. Next, varying the optical power density also enhanced PSC magnitude, reaching 4.24 nA for 808 nm and 0.69 nA for 940 nm at the highest intensity of 266 mW mm-2, as shown in Fig. 3d and 3e. Additionally, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 9a and 9b, increasing the number of pulses at fixed frequency and intensity led to a gradual shift from transient to sustained PSC, demonstrating long-term conductance retention. Quantitative analysis of the gain (An/A1) showed increasing values with both frequency and intensity, reaching maximum values of 4.48 for 808 nm and 2.82 for 940 nm at a higher frequency of 1 Hz, and values of 14.98 for 808 nm and 9.46 for 940 nm at 266 mW mm-2, as shown in Fig. 3f and 3g. These results confirm that Evo-SynT exhibits dynamic modulation of synaptic strength in response to optical stimulation, effectively emulating the transition from STP to LTP observed in biological synapses.

To further evaluate the synaptic functionality of the upconversion-assisted Evo-SynT, repetitive potentiation and depression experiments were carried out under both 808 nm and 940 nm excitation, focusing on the linearity, stability, and bidirectional tunability of conductance modulation. Under 808 nm illumination (13 mW mm-2, 1 Hz), the Evo-SynT exhibited a highly linear increase in conductance across 512 consecutive pulses (Fig. 3h and Supplementary Fig. 10a), demonstrating reliable potentiation with discrete state evolution. This was achieved without any gradual increase in light intensity, which is favorable for low power operation. A similarly robust potentiation trend was observed under 940 nm excitation (Fig. 3j and Supplementary Fig. 10b), confirming consistent behavior across wavelengths.

Depression behavior was investigated by applying a gate bias of 1.5 V for 808 nm and 1.0 V for 940 nm following the optical pulses. To justify these electrical depression conditions, we additionally performed single-pulse transient and relaxation measurements with systematically varied pulse amplitudes and durations, which are provided in the Supplementary Fig. 11. These measurements establish that a pulse duration of 0.5 s with gate biases of 1.5 V (for 808 nm) and 1.0 V (for 940 nm) yields reliable and controlled synaptic depression without inducing excessive over-erasure or instability. For the synaptic weight curves shown in Fig. 3i and 3k, both optical potentiation and electrical depression were implemented using pulse trains at 1 Hz. Optical pulses (808 or 940 nm, 13 mW mm-2) were applied to program LTP, and electrical gate pulses were used to induce long-term depression (LTD). In all cases, the PSC was read out 0.5 s after each pulse to suppress fast transient and capacitive components and to ensure that the extracted values represent quasi-steady synaptic weights, following the protocol commonly used in photonic synapse studies.

As illustrated in Fig. 3i and 3k, the Evo-SynT exhibited symmetric conductance modulation, with PSC values returning to baseline levels in a controlled and reversible manner. To quantitatively assess the linearity of synaptic weight modulation, a nonlinearity (NL) metric was introduced based on exponential fitting of the potentiation and depression characteristics. The weight update behavior under optical stimulation was modeled using the following exponential equations:
GP(t) = B(1-e^(-t/AP)) + GMIN
GD(t) = (GMAX-C)e^(-t/AD) + C

where GP(t) and GD(t) are the conductance during potentiation and depression at time t, respectively, t is the number of optical stimulation pulses, GMAX and GMIN are the maximum and minimum conductance values, respectively, AP and AD are the characteristic nonlinearity parameters for potentiation and depression, respectively, and B and C are fitting constants related to the scaling of conductance range and initial offset. The NL was then calculated as:
NL = tMAX / A

where tMAX is the total number of pulses. Smaller NL values correspond to slower and more linear updates.41,42 Under 808 nm illumination, AP was 360.59 and depression nonlinearity AD was 4290.07, resulting in NL values of 1.42 for potentiation and 0.093 for depression. For 940 nm, AP was 6.63 × 10^6 and AD was 13660.39, with NL values of 7.72 × 10^-5 for potentiation and 0.029 for depression. These findings confirm that the Evo-SynT enables highly linear and symmetric potentiation and depression behaviors across numerous conductance states, making it well suited for precise and scalable synaptic weight modulation in neuromorphic computing platforms.

To further verify that these multilevel synaptic states are not transient artifacts but represent physically stable states, retention measurements were conducted for both optically potentiated and electrically depressed levels, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 12 and 13.54 Distinct synaptic states were first programmed using defined numbers of optical or electrical pulses, and the postsynaptic current was read 10 s after the final pulse to suppress fast transient components. The PSC was then monitored for 100 s and analyzed by linear fitting to evaluate state stability. Using a state-separability criterion based on inter-level spacing, the optically programmed LTP states remained distinguishable for 57 s (64 pulses) up to 795 s (1 pulse) at 808 nm and 68 s (64 pulses) up to 803 s (1 pulse) at 940 nm. For electrical depression, the LTD states remained separable for 70 s (64 pulses) up to 600 s (1 pulse) at 1.5 V and 120 s (64 pulses) up to 900 s (1 pulse) at 1.0 V, confirming stable multilevel electrical erasure with voltage-dependent retention strength.

To evaluate the endurance of the programmed synaptic states under realistic learning conditions, prolonged optical–electrical cycling tests were performed. The Evo-SynT was repeatedly trained using alternating optical potentiation and electrical depression for a total of 1500 cycles, mimicking extended learning and forgetting processes, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 14. Throughout this endurance test, the devices maintained stable and controllable postsynaptic current modulation without abrupt degradation or loss of switching functionality, demonstrating that the UCNP-integrated heterostructure can withstand repeated photo-electrical stress. This result confirms that the multilevel synaptic states are not only retained over time but also preserved under long-term repeated operation, supporting the reliability of the Evo-SynT platform for neuromorphic optoelectronic systems.

These results collectively demonstrate that the Evo-SynT reliably emulates key synaptic behaviors—including STP and LTP, linear and reversible weight modulation, and frequency-dependent learning—under biologically inspired stimulation protocols. Unlike conventional phototransistors, which typically exhibit monotonic and intensity-dependent responses, Evo-SynT shows sensitivity to the temporal dynamics of optical pulses such as frequency, interval, and pulse count. This temporal dependence reflects neuromorphic functionality and distinguishes the Evo-SynT from simple phototransduction-based devices. A performance comparison with recently reported NIR synaptic devices (Supplementary Table 1) confirms that Evo-SynT outperforms existing technologies in terms of responsivity, energy efficiency, and recognition accuracy.

Array integration for in sensor neuromorphic vision
To validate the system-level applicability of the upconversion-assisted Evo-SynT, a 12 × 12-pixel EROS array was constructed on a glass substrate, where each pixel integrates an Evo-SynT and an IGZO-based switching transistor in a two-transistor (2T) configuration, as shown in Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 15a. This architecture enables spatially distributed NIR sensing and synaptic processing across the matrix, supporting precise pixel-level readout and electrical isolation. The vertically stacked IGZO/UCNP/IGZO trilayer structure within each Evo-SynT enhances light absorption while minimizing lateral footprint, yielding a high optical aperture ratio of 70.2% and a geometric fill factor of 35.7%. These features collectively demonstrate a scalable, uniform, and energy-efficient hardware platform for in-sensor neuromorphic vision systems.43

To validate the device fabrication and functionality of the EROS array, photographic and microscope images in Fig. 4b–d and Supplementary Fig. 15b confirm the successful patterning and integration of the optical synaptic pixels, including clearly defined sensing and switching lines across the 12 × 12 matrix. The multilayered device architecture is further detailed in Supplementary Fig. 16, with complete fabrication procedures described in the Methods section. Pixel-wise electrical characterization was performed by applying a 1 V bias to the data line, sweeping the scan line voltage from −10 V to 10 V, and activating the switching transistors using a 5 V gate bias. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 17, the resulting sensing line current (ISL) exhibited uniform and stable characteristics across all pixels, confirming high device yield and reliable operation throughout the array.

To demonstrate neuromorphic functionality at the array level, a cyclic learning-relearning process (learn–forget–1st relearn–forget–2nd relearn) was applied to the EROS array under alternating NIR stimulation. As schematically illustrated in Fig. 4e, optical patterns corresponding to the letters “Y” and “S” were projected onto the array using 808 nm and 940 nm illumination, respectively. Following initial memory encoding, memory decay was induced via dark relaxation, and subsequent reactivation was achieved through relearning cycles. The array was measured using a passive matrix configuration, where conductance changes in individual pixels were read out via line-by-line electrical addressing under scan line voltage 1 V. During each learning and relearning phases, the optical stimulation was applied at a pulse frequency of 1 Hz with a power density of 13 mW mm-2. The 3D surface plot in Fig. 4f displays the ISL distribution across 42 pixels for the “Y” pattern under 808 nm excitation, corresponding to the spatial activation shown in Supplementary Fig. 18a. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 18b, all pixels exceeded the 0.3 nA threshold during initial learning (20 pulses), with reactivation requiring only 5-6 and 3-4 pulses in the first and second relearning cycles, respectively. Supplementary Fig. 19a shows median ISL evolution through dark relaxation (0.01 pA → 0.05 nA → 0.12 nA), while Supplementary Fig. 19b confirms reduced relearning pulse counts (16 → 2-3 → 1-2), collectively indicating stable and cumulative synaptic encoding. A comparable behavior was observed for the “S” pattern under 940 nm excitation, as shown in Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 20a. Supplementary Fig. 20b demonstrates that all 46 addressed pixels exceeded the 0.15 nA threshold, and statistical summaries in Supplementary Fig. 21a and 21b further reveal a progressive increase in median ISL (0.002 nA → 0.040 nA → 0.048 nA) and reduction in pulse counts (17 → 3-4 → 1-2) over successive learning cycles. These results validate the EROS array’s ability to encode, retain, and rapidly recover spatially distributed memory through repeated optical stimulation, underscoring its capability for robust in-sensor learning.

While the current array demonstrates proof-of-concept functionality, its scalability toward high-resolution neuromorphic systems is further addressed in Supplementary Discussion 1, including design strategies to mitigate optical and electrical crosstalk, ensure addressability, and support flexible frame-rate operation. In addition, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 22, the operational reliability of the array under repeated optical–electrical synaptic cycling is quantitatively evaluated, demonstrating stable and reproducible conductance modulation over multiple write–erase sequences, which is essential for large-scale neuromorphic deployment.

Retinocortical near infrared neuromorphic vision computing
To demonstrate the practical utility of the EROS array for real-world vision computing applications, two simulation scenarios were explored: an in-sensor preprocessing task for NIR-based image enhancement under low-light conditions, and an in-memory post-processing task employing transformer-based classification.

As a first step, the in-sensor preprocessing task was implemented to enhance pedestrian detection under low-light conditions by leveraging the EROS array’s NIR sensitivity. As shown in Fig. 5a, the Low Light Visibility Infrared Pedestrian (LLVIP) dataset, containing challenging nighttime visible-light images, was selected to highlight the EROS array's ability to extend visual detection beyond human perception.44 Utilizing experimentally measured optoelectronic characteristics, the device response 𝐼(𝑥) under incident NIR intensity 𝑥 (mW mm-2) was modeled by a second-order polynomial:
𝐼(𝑥) = 𝑎𝑥^2 + 𝑏𝑥 + 𝑐

with fitted coefficients 𝑎 = 4.61×10^-16, 𝑏 = 1.03×10^-12, and 𝑐 = 6.51×10^-11 (808 nm) and 𝑎 = 7.52×10^-17, 𝑏 = 3.81×10^-13, and 𝑐 = 3.45×10^-11 (940 nm). Here, all 𝑥 values directly extracted from the experimental NIR power conditions applied to the physical Evo-SynT devices in EROS array. This approach ensures that the simulated image response is quantitatively grounded in real hardware behavior. For visual representation, raw data were normalized into 8-bit grayscale images via a logarithmic mapping:
𝐺(𝑥) = (log(1 + 𝐼(𝑥)) - log(1 + 𝐼min)) / (log(1 + 𝐼max) - log(1 + 𝐼min)) × 255

This preprocessing strategy, mimicking the neuromorphic visual processing of the EROS array, significantly enhanced pedestrian visibility under low illumination, as depicted in Fig. 5b-d and Supplementary Fig. 23. To quantify effectiveness, pedestrian detection was evaluated using the YOLOv8n model after 50 epochs of training. As shown in Fig. 5e-h, compared with baseline visible images (precision: 0.7806, recall: 0.6407, mean average precision at intersection over union (IoU) threshold 0.5 (mAP@0.5): 0.7190), the NIR-enhanced images under 808 nm illumination yielded marked improvements (precision: 0.8730, recall: 0.7502, mAP@0.5: 0.8481). Further enhancements at 940 nm provided optimal results (precision: 0.9071, recall: 0.8047, mAP@0.5: 0.8869). These findings validate the practical capability of the EROS array to perform intelligent, sensor-level image enhancement, emphasizing its potential as a preprocessing front-end in low-light vision computing systems.

Following the demonstration of EROS array capabilities in preprocessing, its application was further extended to transformer-based image classification using an in-memory computing framework. Employing the Tiny ImageNet dataset for benchmarking, a Vision Transformer (ViT) model was selected due to its complexity and suitability for evaluation (Fig. 6a).46 The experimentally measured potentiation and depression characteristics of the EROS array were mapped onto the transformer's multi-layer perceptron (MLP) synaptic weights, enabling analog weight encoding and low-power inference (Fig. 6b, Supplementary Fig. 24a and 24b). Synaptic programming errors were experimentally characterized for 10 devices under 808 nm and 940 nm illumination as shown in Supplementary Fig. 25a and 25b.47 Linear fitting yielded state-proportional error coefficients (α) of 0.0589 for 808 nm and 0.0767 for 940 nm, with both datasets achieving linearity (R2) greater than 0.9 and remaining within the acceptable error range (α < 8%). The extracted α-values served as direct inputs for the CrossSim inference simulations presented, thereby ensuring that the modeled synaptic variations reproduce experimentally observed programming errors. These results correspond to stable classification accuracy of 77.19% (808 nm) and 79.40% (940 nm), as shown in Fig. 6c–e. Confusion matrices under both wavelengths showed distinct diagonal dominance, indicating robust class discriminability as shown in Fig. 6f and 6g. To provide further granularity, Supplementary Fig. 26 presents class-wise accuracy distributions under both NIR conditions. Notably, the 808 nm case maintains higher accuracy across several classes (e.g., 98%, 96%, 94%), whereas the 940 nm case exhibits slightly more variation with a few lower-performing categories (e.g., 62%, 64%), yet still preserves reliable detectability overall.

The classification results were further analyzed using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE), revealing clearly separated semantic clusters under both illumination conditions as shown in Fig. 6h and 6i. These findings confirm that the EROS array maintains sufficient resolution and linearity of analog weights, effectively supporting transformer-based neuromorphic classification tasks. Overall, the EROS platform successfully demonstrates retinocortical functionality, serving both preprocessing and post-processing roles in integrated neuromorphic vision systems.
paper_content.methods:
Synthesis of NIR responsive NaYF4:Yb/Tm core UCNP
Rare-earth lanthanide precursor solutions were prepared prior to chemical synthesis. YCl3 and YbCl3 were each dissolved in deionized water at a concentration of 1 M, while TmCl3 was prepared at 0.03 M. The solutions were vortexed and sonicated until fully clarified. For the NaOH/NH4F mixture, 0.10 g of NaOH was sonicated in 5 mL of methanol, followed by the addition of 0.148 g of NH4F under vigorous stirring. This solution was freshly prepared for each synthesis.

Under an argon atmosphere, 0.747 mL of YCl3, 0.25 mL of YbCl3, and 0.1 mL of TmCl3 were combined in a 100-mL three-necked round-bottom flask and heated to 110 °C for 15 minutes to evaporate residual water. A magnetic stir bar was used to maintain constant agitation at 300–400 rpm throughout the synthesis. Subsequently, 6 mL of oleic acid and 15 mL of 1-octadecene were added, and the mixture was heated to 150 °C until the solution became a clear pale yellow. After cooling to 60 °C, 5 mL of the methanol-based NaOH/NH4F mixture was introduced. The solution was then heated to 110 °C for 20 minutes to remove methanol, followed by a 10-minute vacuum step to eliminate any residual solvent. Complete removal of methanol and water at this stage is essential to prevent undesirable side reactions. Three consecutive cycles of vacuum and argon purging were conducted, each lasting one minute.

The temperature was increased to 300 °C and maintained for 1 hour under continuous stirring to complete the nanoparticle formation. Upon completion, the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature and transferred to a 50 mL conical tube. The round-bottom flask was rinsed three times with acetone to recover any remaining particles. The total volume in the conical tube was adjusted to 40 mL with acetone and centrifuged at 6,654 g for 10 minutes. The resulting pellet was redispersed in 20 mL of hexane using vortex mixing. A final centrifugation at 1,000 g for 10 minutes was performed, and the clear hexane supernatant containing the nanoparticles was collected into a glass vial.

Fabrication of Evo-SynT
The Evo-SynT devices were fabricated using a three-terminal bottom-gate configuration. A heavily doped p⁺-Si wafer with a thermally grown 120-nm-thick SiO₂ layer served as both the substrate and the gate dielectric, with the underlying silicon functioning as the gate electrode. A 20 nm a-IGZO film was deposited on top of the SiO₂ layer by radio frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering at room temperature under a working pressure of 5 mTorr in argon ambient. The IGZO sputtering target consisted of In2O3:Ga2O3:ZnO in a 1:1:1 molar ratio.

Following the initial IGZO deposition, a layer of UCNPs (NaYF4:Yb/Tm core) was spin-coated onto the IGZO surface at 1000 rpm for 30 s. Subsequently, an additional 20 nm IGZO layer was deposited under identical sputtering conditions, encapsulating the UCNP layer. The stacked IGZO and UCNP layers underwent post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for 1 h and 100 °C for 30 min, respectively.

Finally, aluminium (Al) source and drain electrodes were defined via e-beam evaporation using a precision-aligned shadow mask to form well-defined channels. The resulting devices featured a channel width of 1000 μm and length of 150 μm.

Fabrication of EROS array
To demonstrate the EROS array, thin-film transistor arrays were fabricated on a glass substrate. A chromium (Cr)/gold (Au) (5/45 nm) gate electrode was deposited by thermal evaporation and patterned through a standard photolithography process. Subsequently, as gate insulator, a 55 nm-thick aluminium oxide (Al2O3) layer was deposited by atomic layer deposition process at 150 °C. The channel layer comprises upconversion nanoparticles embedded between two 20 nm-thick IGZO films. Both the top and bottom IGZO layers were deposited by RF magnetron sputtering using an IGZO sputtering target, patterned by photolithography and thermally annealed at 300 °C for 60 min. The UCNPs were spin-coated, patterned by lift off process and thermally annealed 100 °C for 30 min. The Al2O3 layer was patterned using photolithography to form contact holes. Lastly, as source and drain electrodes, a 75 nm-thick Al layer was deposited by thermal evaporation and patterned through a lift-off process. The fabricated TFTs had a channel width and length of 100 μm and 50 μm for Evo-SynT and 100 μm and 10 μm for switching TFT, respectively.

Characterization of UCNP
The characteristics of NaYF4:Yb/Tm core upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) were analyzed using transmission electron microscopy (JEM-F200, JEOL) and field emission scanning electron microscopy (JSM-7610F-Plus, JEOL), along with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy mapping for elemental distribution. Hydrodynamic size was determined via dynamic light scattering using a SZ-100 system (Horiba). Upconversion luminescence spectra were obtained using a Fluorolog-QM photoluminescence spectrometer (Horiba) under excitation by a 980 nm laser.

Device characterization and simulation
The electrical properties of the Evo-SynT devices and EROS array were characterized at room temperature under dark conditions using a parameter analyzer (Model 4200A, Keithley Instruments). To investigate the NIR photoresponse, laser sources (Cubecell Technology) with wavelengths of 808 nm and 940 nm were employed. The incident power densities were systematically varied across seven levels: 13, 127, 255, 510, 764, 1019, and 1325 mW mm-2. To generate pulsed light stimuli, the lasers were modulated through a function/arbitrary waveform generator (UTG1010A, UNI-T), enabling controlled temporal stimulation of the synaptic devices.

To verify the presence and distribution of the NaYF4:Yb/Tm core UCNPs, field emission-scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (JSM-7610F-Plus, JEOL) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping were performed. The upconversion luminescence behavior of the UCNPs was characterized using a photoluminescence spectrometer (FS5, Edinburgh Instruments) under 980 nm laser excitation at a power intensity of 500 mW cm-2. The optical bandgap of the IGZO layer was determined using ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) spectroscopy (V-650, JASCO).

For neuromorphic performance evaluation, a two-stage artificial vision simulation was conducted. In the image pre-processing module, the Low-Light Visibility Infrared Pedestrian (LLVIP) dataset was used in conjunction with the You Only Look Once version 8 nano (YOLOv8n) architecture to enhance visibility under low-light NIR conditions. In the subsequent image classification stage, the Tiny ImageNet dataset was processed using a Vision Transformer (ViT) model within the CrossSim framework to assess the system’s classification accuracy and robustness under varying irradiation conditions.

Schematic illustrations
Schematic illustrations and 3D renderings were created while creating Figure 1a-c, 2c, 2e, 4a, 4e, 5a, 6a, and Supplementary Fig. 3, 6, 15a, 16 using Rhinoceros 3D and KeyShot, and further arranged using Microsoft PowerPoint (Microsoft Corporation).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript introduces the development of a retinal cortex neuromorphological vision platform based on upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) enhanced IGZO synaptic transistors, and its integration into a functional array for near-infrared (NIR) sensing and processing. This work demonstrates the dual-mode operation for image enhancement and classification. However, I found that this work lacks enough novelty. The mechanism explanation of performance is not perfect, and there is a lack of corresponding characterization. In addition, compared with existing neuromorphological vision systems, the proposed application performance does not represent significant progress. For these reasons, I believe that this work should not be published on Nature Communications. Here are some specific opinions.
1.It is recommended to provide a systematic comparison of the absorption spectra of the IGZO thin film, the IGZO/UCNP hybrid structure, and the IGZO/UCNP/IGZO sandwich structure. At present, only the absorption data of the pure IGZO thin film are shown (Supplementary Fig. 4), which is insufficient to demonstrate the effective absorption of upconversion emission or to highlight the design advantage of the IGZO/UCNP/IGZO structure in enhancing light-harvesting efficiency.
2.The authors are advised to carefully check the formatting consistency of all figures throughout the manuscript. Some figures currently show inconsistent fonts, font sizes, and line thicknesses. For example, multiple font sizes are present in Fig. 2h, and the labeling format for the wavelengths “808 nm” and “940 nm” in Figs. 3d and 3e is inconsistent. Standardizing labels, axes, and legends across all figures will significantly improve the clarity and professionalism of the manuscript.
3.In Figs. 3i and 3k, the authors demonstrate synaptic weight depression behavior triggered by electrical pulses, which clearly supports the bidirectional tunability of the device. However, to more comprehensively characterize the electrical synaptic properties, it is suggested to include transfer curves with bidirectional gate voltage sweeps, as well as the transient response and relaxation behavior of the postsynaptic current under single electrical pulses of varying amplitude or duration.
4.The reported near-infrared light power density used in the experiments reached up to 1325 mW/mm², and even the subsequent tests were performed at 13 mW/mm². The accuracy of these values should be clarified. Since practical applications (e.g., automotive night vision) impose strict limits on power consumption and illumination levels, it is recommended to provide device performance data under lower and more realistic power densities. Furthermore, quantifying or citing the upconversion efficiency of UCNPs would help to better evaluate the device performance and energy consumption in real-world conditions.
5.The manuscript lacks statistical analysis of the performance uniformity and reliability of the 12 × 12 EROS array.
6.To highlight the novelty and competitiveness of this work, it is suggested to include a performance comparison table, either in the main text or in the supplementary information, benchmarking the key parameters of this device against those of recently reported devices based on other technologies.
7.In the frequency-dependent experiments presented in Figs. 3b and 3c, the total number of pulses applied varies with frequency. This makes it difficult to attribute the observed differences in excitatory postsynaptic current solely to frequency effects, as they may also arise from differences in the cumulative number of pulses.
8.The description of the electrical testing method for the EROS array is not sufficiently clear. The authors mention that a patterned shadow mask was used for the learning–forgetting–relearning test. How, specifically, was the conductance of the array measured? A more detailed explanation is needed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript proposes a retinocortical in-sensor neuromorphic vision platform for NIR-augmented artificial vision. The work is somewhat intriguing and could be considered for potential publication in Nature Communications after appropriate revisions.
1) Note that the NIR light power densities range from 13 to 1325 mW/mm2. The light irradiation generates a significant amount of heat that seriously affects the device performance. The authors should include a detailed discussion on the impact of such heat.
2) No evidence is provided to support the assertion that the data in Fig. 3i,k indicate the device’s LTP behavior. Retention measurements of different states during the optical potentiation and electrical depression should be conducted, as reported in Ref. [R1]. Additionally, the device current decays over time for both LTP and LTD, indicating that the current data are not constant. This raises the question of how the current data in Fig. 3i,k were obtained. To the best of my knowledge, to date, only Ref. [R1] addresses this issue (see the caption of Fig. 4: “The memconductance values were measured 1 s after each light pulse” and “Top panel: The device was initially set to a relatively low memconductance of about 100 nS, and then ten SET operations were performed with different numbers of 420 nm light pulses. After each SET operation and subsequent retention measurement, the device was set to 100 nS again. Bottom panel: The device was initially set to a relatively high memconductance of about 400 nS, and then ten RESET operations were conducted with different numbers of 800 nm light pulses. After each RESET operation and subsequent retention measurement, the device was set to 400 nS again.”) Therefore, to enhance the scientific rigor of the manuscript, the authors are advised to include a detailed description of the method used to obtain the current data, as outlined in the aforementioned literature.
3) PPC plays a crucial role in mimicking synaptic behaviors. The authors should include a comprehensive discussion on the device’s PPC mechanism. To enhance understanding of the PPC mechanism in oxides, the authors are encouraged to refer to Ref. [R2].
[R1] Adv. Funct. Mater. 2021, 31, 2005582.
[R2] Nat. Mater. 2012, 11, 301-305.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This paper presents an exciting study that combines IGZO transistors with NaYF4:Yb/Tm upconversion nanoparticles to realize an in-sensor neuromorphic vision platform capable of sensing up to the near-infrared (NIR) range. The dual-mode (preprocessing-postprocessing) concept, which mimics the human retina-cortex architecture, is innovative, and the hardware-based demonstration of night vision demonstrates its potential applications. However, further verification is required for the actual photoconversion efficiency of the UCNP-IGZO combination, the identification of the fundamental mechanisms of synaptic activity, and the quantitative reproducibility of the YOLO simulation. Overall, the idea and system integration are excellent, but further experimental evidence and comparative analysis of the data will be necessary to fully support its publication value.
-It is unclear how effectively the upconversion efficiency of NaYF4:Yb/Tm nanoparticles (especially when operated at 808 nm and 940 nm) couples with the actual absorption band of IGZO. A quantitative relationship between the absorption rate of photons emitted from UCNPs, the internal quantum efficiency, and the charge generation efficiency within the IGZO layer needs to be demonstrated experimentally or through simulation. Also physical mechanism should be reinforced.
-In structures where UCNP layers are inserted between IGZO layers, thermal and chemical degradation, ion diffusion, and increased interfacial defects are highly likely to occur during prolonged light irradiation or electrical operation. It is necessary to evaluate whether this structural stability is maintained over long-term repeated operation (thousands of cycles or more), and to evaluate current drift, hysteresis, and fatigue phenomena.
-Although PPC following NIR irradiation was interpreted as synaptic weight maintenance, it could also be explained by a simple phototransduction (trapping–detrapping) phenomenon. It appears that LTP was induced by simple changes in light intensity, without typical pulse-interval-dependent plasticity or voltage-dependent modulation. However, it is important to clarify how synaptic emulation and simple phototransistor operation were distinguished.
-The presented 12 x12 array appears to be a proof-of-concept. System-level limitations, such as optical crosstalk, electrical interference, addressability, and frame rate, that will arise when scaling to higher resolutions are not discussed at all. Design solutions or circuit architecture proposals are needed to address these scalability issues.
-While my paper highlights the advantages of the IGZO-based platform, a direct comparison of actual NIR sensitivity, response speed, SNR, power consumption, and other numerical features with existing 2D materials, perovskite, and organic phototransistor-based NIR devices was not conducted. Performance benchmarking (responsivity, detectivity, retention time) is necessary to truly evaluate the competitiveness of the proposed structure.
-For image detection simulation work, it is unclear whether the data is obtained from actual hardware or is a simple function-fitting-based simulation, and its performance advantage over software has not been clearly proven.

Response to the reviewer #1 comments
This manuscript introduces the development of a retinal cortex neuromorphological vision platform
based on upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) enhanced IGZO synaptic transistors, and its integration
into a functional array for near-infrared (NIR) sensing and processing. This work demonstrates the
dual-mode operation for image enhancement and classification. However, I found that this work lacks
enough novelty. The mechanism explanation of performance is not perfect, and there is a lack of
corresponding characterization. In addition, compared with existing neuromorphological vision
systems, the proposed application performance does not represent significant progress. For these
reasons, I believe that this work should not be published on Nature Communications. Here are some
specific opinions.
 We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful evaluation of our manuscript and for raising
important points regarding novelty, mechanism clarification, and benchmarking. We would like to
clarify that the novelty of this work can be clearly established from 4 complementary perspectives.
1) Conceptual novelty: rarity of NIR-responsive IGZO synaptic transistors.
IGZO thin-film transistors possess a wide bandgap (~3.3 eV), making them intrinsically insensitive
to NIR photons. As a result, only a very limited number of studies (~15 journal papers) have reported
IGZO-based TFTs capable of NIR photodetection, and almost all of these works focus solely on
photodetector functionality. Importantly, among this small body of literature, demonstrations of
synaptic functions such as multi-level plasticity, long-term memory, or bidirectional weight
modulation under NIR stimulation are extremely rare. To the best of our knowledge, this work
represents the first demonstration of an IGZO-based NIR (~940 nm) phototransistor that
simultaneously exhibits synaptic plasticity, analog memory, and array-level operation, establishing a
new device class rather than an incremental extension of existing photodetectors.
2) Mechanistic novelty: UCNP-mediated wavelength conversion instead of heterojunction
charge transfer.
Previous NIR-sensitive IGZO phototransistors rely almost exclusively on hybrid or heterojunction
architectures, where NIR-active absorbers—such as PbS quantum dots, perovskites, other narrow-
bandgap semiconductors, plasmonic nanoparticles, or 2D materials—are directly interfaced with
IGZO to enable interfacial charge transfer. In contrast, our work introduces a fundamentally different
detection mechanism, in which NIR photons are first upconverted by UCNPs into blue/UV photons
that are then absorbed by the IGZO channel itself. This wavelength-conversion strategy enables direct
IGZO photogeneration without interfacial carrier injections, eliminating heterojunction instability
issues and representing the first report of UCNP-enabled NIR sensing in an IGZO synaptic transistor.
3) Quantitative novelty: competitive and benchmarked performance across material
platforms.
Beyond conceptual advances, our device achieves strong quantitative performance, including
high responsivity (116.37 A/W at 808 nm and 57.48 A/W at 940 nm), 512 analog conductance
states, and low energy consumption (77.7 pJ at 808 nm and 25.03 pJ at 940 nm). To place these
results in context, we have added a comprehensive benchmarking table comparing our IGZO-
based platform with state-of-the-art NIR neuromorphic devices based on oxide, 2D, organic, and
perovskite materials. This quantitative comparison demonstrates that the proposed device
achieves a rare combination of NIR sensitivity, analog synaptic resolution, and energy efficiency,
which is not simultaneously realized in prior systems.
4) System-level novelty: scalable array integration and functional application.
Finally, the proposed platform goes beyond single-device demonstrations by integrating a 12 ×
12 synaptic transistor array (288 devices) and validating its statistical reliability, uniformity, and
endurance. This array is further used to demonstrate NIR neuromorphic vision tasks, achieving
84.81% and 90.71% accuracy on the LLVIP dataset under 808 nm and 940 nm illumination,
respectively. Such a complete chain—from NIR sensing and synaptic memory to array-level
processing and application-level performance—has not been demonstrated in prior IGZO-based
or UCNP-assisted neuromorphic systems.
For mechanism explanation, we have significantly strengthened the mechanism analysis by adding
both quantitative metrics and complementary experimental characterizations, thereby clarifying the
physical origin of the observed NIR synaptic behavior.
First, we have added the upconversion quantum yield (UCQY) of the UCNPs and explicitly
incorporated this value into the device-level mechanism analysis. Based on the measured UCQY, we
further calculated the optical coupling efficiency between the UCNP emission and the IGZO
channel, enabling us to quantify how efficiently NIR photons are converted into IGZO-absorbable
photons. This allows us to move beyond a qualitative description of upconversion-assisted sensing and
instead provide a quantitative link between NIR excitation and IGZO photogeneration.
Second, to bridge optical conversion with electrical response, we newly calculated the effective
photon-to-electron conversion factor of the device. This parameter directly connects the number of
NIR photons incident on the device to the number of electrons contributing to the synaptic current,
providing a quantitative measure of the overall optoelectronic transduction pathway from UCNP
upconversion to IGZO conduction. By combining UCQY, optical coupling efficiency, effective photon-
to-electron conversion factor, the full mechanism is now supported by a closed, quantitative framework,
rather than by phenomenological interpretation alone.
Third, we added UV–Vis–NIR absorption spectra for each device configuration. These data directly
verify the spectral matching between UCNP emission and IGZO absorption and confirm that the
observed NIR response cannot arise from IGZO alone. This spectral evidence further validates the
proposed upconversion-mediated mechanism.
Finally, we have expanded the discussion by incorporating newly added, recent journal references that
report related upconversion-assisted photodetection and oxide-based synaptic mechanisms, allowing
the proposed mechanism to be placed in a broader and more rigorous context.
We respectfully note that the concerns raised by the reviewer regarding novelty, mechanism, and
benchmarking have been fully and systematically addressed in this revision. Specifically, we have
clarified the unique novelty of this work, strengthened the mechanistic explanation with new
quantitative and spectroscopic characterizations, and added comprehensive benchmarking and ablation
analyses to contextualize the application-level performance. We therefore kindly ask the reviewer to
reconsider the evaluation of this manuscript based on the revised version, which now provides a
complete and rigorously supported presentation of the proposed NIR neuromorphic vision platform.
Comment 1: It is recommended to provide a systematic comparison of the absorption spectra of the
IGZO thin film, the IGZO/UCNP hybrid structure, and the IGZO/UCNP/IGZO sandwich structure. At
present, only the absorption data of the pure IGZO thin film are shown (Supplementary Fig. 4), which
is insufficient to demonstrate the effective absorption of upconversion emission or to highlight the
design advantage of the IGZO/UCNP/IGZO structure in enhancing light-harvesting efficiency.
Reply
 We agree with the reviewer that a comparative analysis of the absorption characteristics across
different structural configurations is important to clarify the optoelectronic advantage of the
IGZO/UCNP/IGZO architecture. In response, we have newly conducted UV–Vis–NIR absorption
measurements on three structures: (i) pristine IGZO thin film, (ii) IGZO/UCNP bilayer, and (iii)
IGZO/UCNP/IGZO trilayer, to make a systematic comparison of the absorption spectra under NIR
region. The results are presented in Fig. R1.
As shown, the pristine IGZO layer exhibits negligible absorbance at 808 nm and 940 nm, consistent
with its wide bandgap nature and minimal interaction with NIR photons. In contrast, both hybrid
structures incorporating UCNPs show clear absorption features at these wavelengths, verifying their
capacity to harvest NIR light. Notably, the IGZO/UCNP/IGZO sandwich structure displays enhanced
absorbance over the IGZO/UCNP bilayer, attributable to increased optical confinement and improved
vertical coupling with the UCNP layer. These findings confirm that the designed trilayer architecture
significantly improves the NIR light-harvesting capability.
Beyond optical efficiency, the trilayer design also addresses device performance and fabrication
challenges. In the bilayer IGZO/UCNP structure, UCNP particles are positioned at the IGZO–electrode
interface, which interferes with uniform carrier injection and transistor operation due to surface
roughness and nonuniform contact morphology.
By contrast, the IGZO/UCNP/IGZO configuration separates the UCNPs from the electrical contacts,
allowing the top and bottom IGZO layers to serve as both optical sensitizers and stable transistor
channels. This vertically stacked geometry ensures direct IGZO–electrode contact while still enabling
photon absorption via upconverted emission from the embedded UCNPs. Similar multilayered hybrid
configurations have been shown to improve both light-matter interaction and carrier transport in
advanced phototransistor designs.1-3
We have added comparative absorption data in supplementary information and incorporated a
structural benchmarking discussion into the revised manuscript to clarify the design advantages of the
IGZO/UCNP/IGZO configuration.
Fig. R1. NIR absorbance spectra of three structures: (i) pristine IGZO thin film, (ii) IGZO/UCNP
bilayer, and (iii) IGZO/UCNP/IGZO trilayer.

Comment 3: In Figs. 3i and 3k, the authors demonstrate synaptic weight depression behavior triggered
by electrical pulses, which clearly supports the bidirectional tunability of the device. However, to more
comprehensively characterize the electrical synaptic properties, it is suggested to include transfer
curves with bidirectional gate voltage sweeps, as well as the transient response and relaxation behavior
of the postsynaptic current under single electrical pulses of varying amplitude or duration.
Reply
 In response to the reviewer’s request, we have now newly added electrical synaptic properties
including transfer curve with bidirectional gate voltage sweeps, transient response, and relaxation
behavior of the postsynaptic current to further strengthen the physical understanding and completeness
of the device operation.
1) Transfer curve with bidirectional gate voltage sweep:
We have measured transfer curve with bidirectional gate voltage sweep, which are now
provided in Fig. R2. The device exhibits a clear clockwise hysteresis loop with a positive
threshold-voltage shift between forward and reverse sweeps, which is characteristic of IGZO-
based TFTs. The extracted threshold-voltage shift (~1 V) is comparable to that of pristine
IGZO TFTs and is consistent with trap-mediated charge storage associated with oxygen-
vacancy-related states under electrical bias.1,2
Importantly, however, electrical pulses alone do not generate or modulate a synaptic state in
our device. Synaptic depression is observed only after prior optical potentiation, indicating
that the electrical response is gated by an optically written memory rather than by intrinsic
IGZO hysteresis. Thus, while the bidirectional transfer curves confirm normal IGZO TFT
behavior, the transient electrical depression verifies the unique photo-enabled synaptic
operation.
Fig. R2. Transfer characteristics of Evo-SynT under bidirectional gate voltage sweep.
2) Electrical transient and relaxation behavior under single electrical pulse:
We additionally measured the postsynaptic current transient and relaxation behavior under
single electrical depression pulses with systematically varied amplitude and duration.
Specifically, the device was first optically potentiated by 808 nm illumination at 13 mW/mm2
for 10 s, followed by a 10 s relaxation period before applying the electrical depression pulse.
(i) Varying electrical pulse amplitude (pulse width fixed at 1 s)
Electrical depression pulses of 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 V were applied, and the corresponding
postsynaptic current evolution is shown in Fig. R3. The results show a clear and systematic
dependence on pulse amplitude.
When a 1.0 V electrical pulse was applied, the postsynaptic current exhibited a moderate
decrease, dropping to approximately 0.11 nA immediately after the pulse and then slowly
relaxing to a stable value of about 0.10 nA after 70 s, indicating weak but sustained synaptic
depression. Increasing the pulse amplitude to 1.5 V induced a stronger depression, with the
current decreasing to around 0.08 nA right after the pulse and gradually relaxing to
approximately 0.07 nA over 70 s, demonstrating enhanced electrical erase strength. At a higher
amplitude of 2.0 V, a much more pronounced response was observed. The current initially
dropped sharply to about 0.02 nA, followed by a partial recovery and saturation near 0.05 nA,
before finally stabilizing at approximately 0.04 nA. This non-monotonic transient behavior
reflects the strong electric-field–induced redistribution of optically stored charges, followed
by re-equilibration of shallow and deep trap states.
Overall, the monotonic decrease of the residual postsynaptic current with increasing pulse
amplitude demonstrates voltage-controlled depression strength, fully consistent with synaptic
weight modulation in oxide-based neuromorphic transistors.
Fig. R3. Electrical synaptic depression and relaxation of Evo-SynT under single-pulse voltage
stimulation with varying amplitude.
(ii) Varying electrical pulse duration (amplitude fixed at 1.5 V)

Comment 7: In the frequency-dependent experiments presented in Figs. 3b and 3c, the total number of
pulses applied varies with frequency. This makes it difficult to attribute the observed differences in
excitatory postsynaptic current solely to frequency effects, as they may also arise from differences in the
cumulative number of pulses.
Reply
 We appreciate the reviewer’s concern. We respectfully clarify that using a fixed stimulation window
while varying pulse frequency is a well-established approach in neuromorphic synapse research and is
biologically relevant. In real neurons, higher firing rates within a given time lead to greater postsynaptic
responses due to temporal summation – successive EPSCs overlap when inter-spike intervals are short,
so the responses accumulate instead of fully resetting between spikes. Our stimulation protocol was
designed to capture this frequency-dependent facilitation rather than simply deliver more total pulses.
In other words, keeping the time constant isolates how pulse timing (rate) affects synaptic output, which
is a hallmark of biological synapses (frequent spikes elevate the baseline and produce larger subsequent
currents before the synapse can return to baseline).
Multiple studies have employed similar protocols to demonstrate frequency-dependent synaptic
plasticity in hardware devices.1-4 A similar methodology was adopted by Mei et al., where they
demonstrated frequency-dependent synaptic plasticity in an organic optoelectronic synapse by applying
light pulse trains over fixed durations. Specifically, they delivered spike trains with different pulse
intervals—3 s, 4 s, and 7 s—each within the same total stimulation time window, thereby modulating
the input frequency. The resulting EPSC amplitudes increased with higher stimulation frequency,
attributed to the temporal overlap and accumulation of individual responses. This protocol closely
mirrors biological mechanisms, where firing rate within a given period governs synaptic strength. Their
approach reinforces that using a fixed time window with varying frequency is a biologically relevant
and experimentally justified method to evaluate frequency-dependent plasticity in neuromorphic
devices.1
Likewise, Xu et al. reported that in a multiterminal synaptic transistor, keeping the stimulation period
constant while increasing spike frequency led to much greater potentiation. In their device, pike trains
of varying frequencies (e.g., 0.5 Hz to 10 Hz) were applied over the same 20-second duration, and the
resulting EPSC showed a dramatic increase with frequency—for instance, higher-frequency stimulation
(10 Hz) led to a significantly larger synaptic current compared to low-frequency input (0.5 Hz)—
attributed to the cumulative overlap of EPSCs within the fixed time window, effectively mimicking
biological facilitation.2
Our own data reflects a similar trend: at higher input frequencies, the EPSC does not fully decay
between pulses, resulting in an elevated baseline and larger successive responses. This behavior is
consistent with previously reported observations and suggests that our device captures frequency-
dependent summation effects. While increasing frequency within a fixed time window naturally leads
to a greater number of pulses, this protocol is arguably more faithful to biological synaptic behavior
than fixing pulse count—since real neurons typically modulate synaptic strength through changes in
firing rate over time. Accordingly, we believe our approach provides a biologically relevant and
experimentally valid means of evaluating frequency-dependent plasticity in neuromorphic systems.

Reply
 Retention measurements for different synaptic states during both optical potentiation and electrical
depression were newly conducted, following a protocol directly comparable to Ref. [R1], and are now
provided in Fig. R11 and R12.
For optical potentiation, distinct synaptic states were programmed by applying a controlled number of
NIR light pulses (808 nm or 940 nm) with identical pulse conditions (power density: 13 mW/mm2 ,
frequency: 1 Hz), as shown in Fig. R11. To ensure that the extracted PSC values represent steady
synaptic weights, we defined the readout point as 10 s after the final optical pulse. This deliberate delay
suppresses fast photocarrier relaxation and excludes short-lived components immediately following
illumination. After this readout, the PSC was continuously monitored for 100 s under the same electrical
bias to evaluate the retention behavior of each programmed LTP level.
Because gradual current decay is intrinsic to oxide-based photonic synapses, the retention traces were

Reviewer #3 Comments:
This paper presents an exciting study that combines IGZO transistors with NaYF4:Yb/Tm upconversion
nanoparticles to realize an in-sensor neuromorphic vision platform capable of sensing up to the near-
infrared (NIR) range. The dual-mode (preprocessing-postprocessing) concept, which mimics the human
retina-cortex architecture, is innovative, and the hardware-based demonstration of night vision
demonstrates its potential applications. However, further verification is required for the actual
photoconversion efficiency of the UCNP-IGZO combination, the identification of the fundamental
mechanisms of synaptic activity, and the quantitative reproducibility of the YOLO simulation. Overall,
the idea and system integration are excellent, but further experimental evidence and comparative
analysis of the data will be necessary to fully support its publication value.
1. It is unclear how effectively the upconversion efficiency of NaYF4:Yb/Tm nanoparticles (especially
when operated at 808 nm and 940 nm) couples with the actual absorption band of IGZO. A quantitative
relationship between the absorption rate of photons emitted from UCNPs, the internal quantum
efficiency, and the charge generation efficiency within the IGZO layer needs to be demonstrated
experimentally or through simulation. Also physical mechanism should be reinforced.
2. In structures where UCNP layers are inserted between IGZO layers, thermal and chemical
degradation, ion diffusion, and increased interfacial defects are highly likely to occur during prolonged
light irradiation or electrical operation. It is necessary to evaluate whether this structural stability is
maintained over long-term repeated operation (thousands of cycles or more), and to evaluate current
drift, hysteresis, and fatigue phenomena.
3. Although PPC following NIR irradiation was interpreted as synaptic weight maintenance, it could
also be explained by a simple phototransduction (trapping–detrapping) phenomenon. It appears that
LTP was induced by simple changes in light intensity, without typical pulse-interval-dependent
plasticity or voltage-dependent modulation. However, it is important to clarify how synaptic
emulation and simple phototransistor operation were distinguished.
4. The presented 12 x12 array appears to be a proof-of-concept. System-level limitations, such as optical
crosstalk, electrical interference, addressability, and frame rate, that will arise when scaling to higher
resolutions are not discussed at all. Design solutions or circuit architecture proposals are needed to
address these scalability issues.
5. While my paper highlights the advantages of the IGZO-based platform, a direct comparison of actual
NIR sensitivity, response speed, SNR, power consumption, and other numerical features with existing
2D materials, perovskite, and organic phototransistor-based NIR devices was not conducted.
Performance benchmarking (responsivity, detectivity, retention time) is necessary to truly evaluate the
competitiveness of the proposed structure.
6. For image detection simulation work, it is unclear whether the data is obtained from actual hardware
or is a simple function-fitting-based simulation, and its performance advantage over software has not
been clearly proven.

Comment 3: Although PPC following NIR irradiation was interpreted as synaptic weight maintenance,
it could also be explained by a simple phototransduction (trapping–detrapping) phenomenon. It
appears that LTP was induced by simple changes in light intensity, without typical pulse-interval-
dependent plasticity or voltage-dependent modulation. However, it is important to clarify how synaptic
emulation and simple phototransistor operation were distinguished.
Reply
 The observed LTP and PPC behaviors in our device are not solely the result of simple phototransistor
dynamics. Rather than being induced by mere changes in light intensity, the LTP characteristics emerge
from the application of temporally structured pulse trains with defined frequency, pulse number, and
inter-pulse interval—protocols designed to emulate biologically inspired synaptic stimulation. As
shown in Fig. 3b–g and revised Supplementary Fig. 9, the synaptic weight enhancement exhibits clear
dependencies on pulse frequency and count, aligning with cumulative learning behaviors commonly
observed in neural systems. These trends differ from the immediate and largely reversible photocurrent
responses typically associated with conventional phototransistors.
Furthermore, the PPC observed in our device is not explained by shallow trap-based trapping–
detrapping dynamics. As discussed in the main text (page 6~7) and illustrated in revised
Supplementary Fig. 6, the PPC arises from the ionization of deep-level neutral oxygen vacancies (V )
O
within IGZO, which release electrons and form metastable donor states (V + and V 2+) upon absorption
O O
of blue and UV photons upconverted from NIR-excited UCNPs. These ionized states exhibit long
lifetimes due to kinetic barriers to recombination, leading to slow decay and enabling analog retention
of optical memory—an essential feature of neuromorphic behavior.1
While phototransistors typically respond to light via simple, monotonic photocurrent generation with
limited temporal sensitivity, our Evo-SynT exhibits hallmark features of synaptic function that cannot
be explained by phototransduction alone:
1) Paired-pulse facilitation (PPF): As shown in Fig. 3a, our device exhibits a clear
exponential decay in the PPF index with increasing inter-spike interval (Δt), which closely
mirrors biological short-term plasticity. Such Δt-dependent facilitation is not observed in
conventional phototransistor operation, where photocurrent is independent of pulse timing.
2) Cumulative transition from STP to LTP: Fig. 3b–g and revised Supplementary Fig. 9
demonstrate that repeated optical stimulation leads to a gradual and nonlinear increase in
postsynaptic current (PSC), consistent with a short-term to long-term potentiation
transition. This behavior reflects cumulative memory formation, which does not arise from
individual trap dynamics in basic phototransistors.
3) Bidirectional, analog weight modulation: Fig. 3h–k illustrate that the Evo-SynT enables
multi-level potentiation via NIR light and reversible depression via electrical pulses,
allowing symmetric and analog tuning across 512 conductance states. Such precise
bidirectional control is beyond the capability of typical phototransistors, which lack
electrical reversibility or multilevel weight states.
Collectively, these results confirm that the Evo-SynT operates beyond the scope of simple
phototransistor behavior and functions as a neuromorphic device with biologically relevant plasticity
mechanisms. To emphasize this distinction, we have now revised the manuscript text accordingly to
highlight the spatiotemporal and bidirectional control features that underpin true synaptic emulation.

Reply
 We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the scalability of the 12 × 12 EROS
array. While large-scale integration was not the primary focus of the present study, we fully agree that
a discussion of system-level limitations and architectural considerations is essential to evaluate the
feasibility of implementing the proposed retinocortical vision platform in real-world applications.
To address this point, we have added a dedicated paragraph to the Discussion section outlining how
the key scalability concerns—optical crosstalk, electrical interference, addressability, and frame rate—
can be mitigated or accommodated by design. Our summary is as follows:
1) Optical crosstalk: The vertically stacked IGZO/UCNP/IGZO structure inherently confines
light absorption to the subpixel region. In addition, the surrounding metal interconnects
act as lateral optical shields. For higher-resolution implementations, further measures such
as patterned optical shielding layers1, or microlens arrays2 could be adopted to suppress
lateral photon leakage between adjacent pixels.
2) Electrical interference: Each pixel contains a dedicated switching transistor that provides
per-pixel isolation during readout. Standard mitigation techniques used in active-matrix
architectures, such as ground shielding3, and differential sensing4, can be implemented to
reduce parasitic coupling and ensure signal integrity across large arrays.
3) Addressability: The current pixel design follows a passive-matrix compatible row/column
scheme, which can be directly adapted into an active-matrix architecture using well-
established TFT driver circuitry.5 This ensures that the addressing protocol scales linearly
with resolution, as in conventional flat-panel displays and imagers.
4) Fram rate: The achievable frame rate is determined by the array readout speed and the
intrinsic time constants of the EROS array. Importantly, the device’s plasticity timescale
can be tuned by adjusting optical or electrical stimulation parameters, allowing the
platform to be configured for either high-speed sensing (e.g., real-time image capture) or
slow-memory operation (e.g., adaptive vision), depending on application needs.6
These system-level design considerations have now been incorporated into the revised supplementary
information to clarify that the current implementation serves as a scalable foundation. The Evo-SynT
pixel architecture is inherently compatible with high-density integration, and the EROS platform can
be extended toward larger formats through standard circuit and packaging techniques. This update
directly addresses the reviewer’s concerns by providing a practical roadmap for scaling the device
toward functional neuromorphic vision systems.
